editorNote: A British courtroom challenge puts game cloning on the front page while Atari's new ownership moves quickly, Apple prepares more Macintoshes, and 1200-baud modems edge toward mass-market prices.
morningLine: Game makers test the boundaries of copying as Atari reorganizes and Apple turns up the Macintosh line.

lead.headline: Activision Forces 'Cuthbert in the Jungle' Off the Market
lead.dek: A High Court undertaking pulls Microdeal's Commodore 64 game from sale and makes the young software trade confront the difference between inspiration and imitation.
body: LONDON — Activision has forced Microdeal to withdraw Cuthbert in the Jungle after bringing High Court proceedings that alleged the Commodore 64 title copied Pitfall!, Popular Computing Weekly reported on July 26. Microdeal gave the court an undertaking that it would no longer produce the game in any form and notified suppliers that the title could no longer be sold.

Activision UK managing director Geoff Heath said his company had first asked Microdeal to remove the game before turning to legal action. The dispute puts unusual public pressure on a trade in which successful arcade and home-computer designs are often followed quickly by close variations, sometimes with only their names and scenery changed.

Microdeal had already encountered a similar challenge. Nintendo objected the previous year to the firm's Donkey King, after which the game was renamed The King. This week's result suggests that a change of title may not settle complaints when a publisher believes the play itself follows a protected hit too closely.

The magazine's editorial widened the argument beyond one program, criticizing an industry that condemns cassette piracy while tolerating catalogs crowded with near-copies. For buyers, programmers, and small publishers, the Cuthbert undertaking is an early warning that software law may now shape what reaches the shelves as strongly as memory limits and machine compatibility.

stories.headline: Tramiel's Atari Shake-Up Reaches Britain
body: Atari's change of control is already remaking its British operation. Popular Computing Weekly reported that UK managing director Graham Clark resigned and that many sales and management employees were dismissed, with financial controller Simon Westbrook serving as acting managing director.

Several former Commodore executives joined Jack Tramiel's organization as the new owners moved to streamline the loss-making company. The reported plan was to replace much of Atari's own sales force with appointed distributors.

Across the Atlantic, Electronic Games Hotline said previously announced products had been put on hold for several weeks while management reviewed fall plans. The pause leaves dealers and players waiting to learn which machines and games will survive the transition.

stories.headline: Apple Plans to Double Macintosh Production
body: Apple plans to double Macintosh production by the end of 1984, according to Electronic Games Hotline. The Fremont, California, factory was reported to be turning out about 40,000 machines each month.

Chief executive John Sculley also said that a Macintosh with expanded memory would appear during the year, though he offered no specifications. Six months after the machine's launch, the announcement signals that Apple expects demand to carry the compact graphical computer beyond its first wave of enthusiasts.

stories.headline: A Computer Fantasy Game Becomes an Alan Dean Foster Novel
body: The usual book-to-game path is running backward: Ultrasoft's Shadowkeep, published on Spinnaker's Trillium label, has inspired a forthcoming novel by science-fiction author Alan Dean Foster.

The illustrated fantasy game supports as many as nine players, with five character classes and four races. Creatures drawn from Welsh and Scottish mythology, high-resolution graphics, animation, and a parser accepting full sentences give the project enough of a world to travel from disk to printed page.

briefs.headline: McGraw-Hill buys Future Computing
briefs.summary: McGraw-Hill acquired the PC research and consulting firm for an undisclosed cash price; the buyer cited a market growing from $10 billion in 1983 toward a forecast $40 billion in 1988.

market.headline: Atari's New Owners Cut and Reconsider
market.summary: The British sales organization is being stripped back as Tramiel's team reviews announced products and prepares a distributor-led operation.

worldAnchor.headline: Los Angeles Olympics open amid Soviet-led boycott
worldAnchor.summary: President Reagan opened the Games on July 28; the first day of competition brought six U.S. gold medals while the Soviet-led boycott and Libya's last-minute withdrawal remained part of the story.

bbsNote.headline: 1200-Baud Modems Fall Below the Old $500 Barrier
bbsNote.summary: PC Magazine's July 24 ads make the economics of going online unusually concrete: Hayes's external Smartmodem 1200 remained near $500, while Qubie pitched a $299 internal PC package built around four signal-processing chips and Hayes-compatible commands.

posts.text: Qubie's PC212A/1200 card bundled PC-TALK III, modular cable, quick-reference card and manual for $299; an optional external serial-port connector cost $20.
A dealer offered the Hayes Smartmodem 300 at $209, Smartmodem 1200 at $489, and internal 1200B with Smartcom II at $419.
Knowledge Industry Publications charged $185 annually for its directory and online service, including $75 usage; additional access ran $60 per hour with a $7 minimum.

curiosity.headline: An Arcade Cabinet with Three Joysticks and a Seat That Shakes
curiosity.summary: Mylstar supplied two gloriously excessive arcade ideas in one week's newsletter: a Three Stooges cabinet with a joystick for each Stooge and a laser-game conversion with vibrating-seat effects.
curiosity.detail: The Three Stooges let one to three players slap villains and throw pies through 28 rounds. Mylstar's Us vs. Them conversion for M.A.C.H. 3 mixed live-action footage, superimposed graphics, an orchestral score and a vibrating seat to simulate flight.
